question: Before anyone presses an oil, what do people cook, burn and anoint with — and where do the first oil crops come from?
thesis: From 8000 to 1200 BC fat splits into two stories: an animal story of rendering, milk and the first butter across the herding world, and a plant story of the olive, sesame and flax pressed into oil from the Levant to the Indus. The plant evidence is firmer, the animal evidence mostly textual, and Africa, the Americas, China and the Pacific enter only at the margins.

big_ideas.title: Milk gives the first manufactured fat
big_ideas.text: Herders who milk sheep and goats end up with butter, clarified in hot lands into the ancestor of ghee. But milking cannot be assumed from the start of domestication, the Indus pots hold animal fat with little sign of dairy, and China keeps pigs for fat and no milk at all.

big_ideas.title: The olive becomes an economy
big_ideas.text: The tree is domesticated in the Chalcolithic Levant; by the Late Bronze Age palaces at Ebla, Mari, Ugarit and Crete store oil in bulk, Cyprus and Crete press it at scale, and inspectors already police the growers and millers. Oil is the first fat to be traded and taxed.

big_ideas.title: Sesame is the oil that travels
big_ideas.text: Sesame is a crop of the Indus by 2600 BC, reaches Mesopotamia within a few centuries with its names, and turns up in Tutankhamun’s tomb. The cuneiform ‘oil-plant’ and Egypt’s nhh are still argued over, and a Neolithic sesame in China is doubted.

big_ideas.title: Many peoples press seeds of their own
big_ideas.text: Flax, mustard and rape, poppy, Camelina, soy, sunflower and peanut each enter the record in a different place, often as a seed whose oil use is inferred. The Fertile Crescent’s olive and sesame story is the best documented, not the only one.

big_ideas.title: Climate and herds decide which fat
big_ideas.text: Animal fat in the cool north and plant oil in the warm south is the baseline; where the tsetse fly or the lack of domesticates left few herds, tree fats such as the avocado, the oil palm and Pacific nuts take their place, and northern foragers keep burning and cooking marine fat.

threads.title: Milk, butter and animal fat
threads.claim: Butter is invented by Neolithic herders, but the record is patchy and who milked, and when, is argued.

beats.text: Neolithic herders make the first butter, from sheep, goat and yak milk, and not at first on purpose.
Rendering, heating tissue until the fat separates, is the oldest way to extract fat.
Milk fat is absorbed in Saharan pots at Takarkori, the herders’ dairying of the green Sahara.
China keeps pigs and dogs for meat and fat from Yangshao to Shang, and does not use milk.
Sherratt argues that animals were first kept for meat and milked only some millennia later.
Fuller notes that archaeologists often assume cattle mean milk, but cattle are not universally milked.
Indus pots hold degraded animal fat, with little sign of dairy.
In Mesopotamia butter is always clarified, so that it keeps in the heat.
The Yale tablets build almost every dish from water, then fat, then aromatics.

threads.title: The olive and its oil
threads.claim: From a domesticated Levantine tree to palace cellars and Cretan exports.

beats.text: Charred stones and wood at Tuleilat Ghassul show the olive domesticated in the Chalcolithic Levant.
Cuneiform tablets from Ebla record inspectors checking olive growers and millers for fraud.
Oil fills the earthenware jars in the palace cellars of Ebla, Mari, Ugarit and Minoan Crete.
Cyprus and Crete press olives at scale.
Crete grows rich on exported oil.

threads.title: Sesame from the Indus to the Nile
threads.claim: A crop domesticated in South Asia becomes the Near East’s prestige oil within a thousand years.

beats.text: Sesame, peanuts and broad beans are reported from a Chekiang Neolithic layer, a find few believe.
A lump of charred sesame at Harappa shows it an established Indus crop.
Sesame reaches Mesopotamia, and the Sumerian and Akkadian names for the oil resemble early Dravidian names for the plant.
Cuneiform texts name an ‘oil-plant’, šamaššammū, which scholars dispute between sesame and flax.
Sixty millilitres of sesame lie among the grave goods in Tutankhamun’s Annexe.
Egyptian texts name nhh as the best oil; whether it is sesame, castor or something else is unknown.

threads.title: Egypt’s fats, as Lucas read them
threads.claim: Egypt pressed its own native oils, imported its olive oil, and has been wrongly credited with palm fat.

beats.text: Egypt grows ben, balanos and castor for oil.
The palm fat said to be in a tomb at Abydos rests on one analysis of 1897 that Lucas rejects.
Egypt’s ‘butter’ is butter fat, alongside ox fat, goose fat and cheese.
The olive is seldom named in Egypt’s records: a sacred tree at Heliopolis and oil from Syria.
Canaanite oil goes to Egypt, with olive stones aboard the Uluburun ship.

threads.title: Other oil seeds, in other places
threads.claim: Seeds for oil are domesticated or collected in many places, and most of the evidence shows the seed, not the pressing.

beats.text: Flax, about 40 per cent oil, is one of the founder crops of south-west Asia.
Crushed Brassica or Sinapis cakes lie at Jerf el Ahmar; wild crucifers are collected in Swiss lake villages.
Brassica seeds at Banpo in Shaanxi may have been used for oil, or only as greens.
The opium poppy, a seed for oil as well as latex, spreads from La Marmotta to the Alpine lakes.
Camelina, a weed of flax, becomes central Europe’s oil crop, from Auvernier to the Baltic coast.
Mustard and linseed turn up at the Harappan sites.
The soybean is domesticated in north-east China, by a date argued between 2700 and 1000 BC.
The sunflower is domesticated in eastern North America.
Peanuts are grown in Peru.

threads.title: Beyond the Fertile Crescent: sea, climate and tree fats
threads.claim: Where herds or oilseeds were missing, people used fruit trees, nuts and the sea.

beats.text: Kiple’s editors say the tsetse belt and the Americas had few herds, so tree fats filled the gap.
At El Gigante in Honduras people manage the avocado and select for bigger, thicker-skinned fruit.
Late Mesolithic hunters of the Ertebølle culture burn blubber in small lamps.
In the western Baltic about one pot in five still cooks marine and freshwater food as farming arrives.
Climate sets the fat: animal fat in the north, plant oil in the south.
Canarium almond, coconut and candlenut are preserved in waterlogged sites of Near Oceania.
Oil-palm shells are reported from sites in West and Central Africa, on one unverified abstract.

turning_points.text: Neolithic herders make the first butter.
Flax is an early oil and fibre crop in south-west Asia.
The olive is domesticated in the Levant.
Milking is argued to come late, not with the first herds.
Sesame is an established crop of the Indus.
Ebla’s inspectors police the olive trade.
Cyprus and Crete press olives at scale.
The Yale tablets set fat in the pot of the oldest recipes.
Sesame is among Tutankhamun’s grave goods.

text: Europe enters through the island palaces of Crete and Cyprus, where oil is pressed at scale ([[ec8]], [[te2]]), and through the northern oil seeds read from Zohary’s archaeobotany: the poppy from La Marmotta to the lake villages, and Camelina from Auvernier to the Baltic ([[ec26]], [[ec25]]). The north’s animal-fat world is described in the climate baseline ([[w1]]), and the sea fat of the Baltic is here too: marine and freshwater food in pots and the blubber lamps of the Late Mesolithic ([[ec15]], [[te4]]). Nothing in the library dates a European animal-fat practice before 1200 BC.

The core of the folio, because the evidence is here: the first butter and clarified butter, the Chalcolithic olive, flax, palace oil stores, the Babylonian recipes and the inspectors of Ebla ([[ec1]], [[ec2]], [[ec3]], [[ec9]], [[e1]], [[o1]]). Egypt is filed under the Near East in the atlas, though it is African: butter fat and the cheese at Saqqara, ben, balanos and castor oils, the rare olive, Tutankhamun’s sesame, nhh and the contested Abydos palm fat ([[ec19]], [[ec20]], [[ec21]], [[x2]], [[th2]], [[ec7]]), and Canaanite oil on the sea routes to Egypt ([[x4]]). Beeswax in Turkish pots from about 7000 BC is here as a lipid used later for candles and seals ([[ec16]]). Crushed brassica or mustard seed cakes at Jerf el Ahmar and carbonised seeds at Khafadje are the earliest hints of pressed or ground oil seeds ([[ec27]]).

The Harappan Indus: sesame, mustard and linseed, animal fat in the pots, and Fuller’s caution about assuming milk ([[ec4]], [[ec5]], [[ec17]], [[th3]]), with sesame’s journey west ([[x1]]). China has three entries: pigs and dogs for meat and fat with no milk, the doubted sesame and peanuts of Chekiang, and the soybean, whose domestication date (2700 or 1000 BC) is argued ([[ec22]], [[th5]], [[ec14]]). China’s earliest possible oil crop is also here: brassica seeds at Banpo, which may have been pressed ([[ec24]]).

Two entries, both at the thin end of the evidence: dairy fat in Saharan pots ([[ec10]]) and oil-palm shells at West and Central African sites ([[ec11]]). Egypt’s entries sit under the Near East, among them the correction of the Abydos palm claim ([[ec7]]). Nothing in the library covers shea, Ethiopian oilseeds or the Nile above Egypt in this period.

Five entries: the managed avocado at El Gigante, peanuts grown in Peru by 2000 BC with Kiple’s note that the New World had few fat animals, the sunflower domesticated in eastern North America, Moseley’s own finding that preceramic Peru’s coast lived mainly on marine protein — though sea lion itself was rare, the sea’s main gift was fish, shellfish and birds — and the high puna around Lake Junín, where camelid hunting rose as deer fell and broken bone grew more common, read as marrow and grease extraction, until domestication appears by about 2000 BC ([[ec23]], [[ec12]], [[ec28]], [[ec13]], [[ec29]]).
One entry: coconut, Canarium almond and candlenut at waterlogged New Guinea sites, 3800 to 2100 BC, from Kirch ([[ec18]]). They are fat-bearing nuts; nothing says oil was pressed.

The climate baseline that sets the fat by the land, Sherratt’s hypothesis on when people began to milk, and Kiple’s editors on why Africa south of the Sahara and the Americas, with few herds, lean on tree fats ([[w1]], [[th4]], [[th6]]).

sources.intro: Prehistory is a story of plants and pots, so the folio leans on botanical syntheses, specialist volumes on sesame, and a translation of the Babylonian cooking tablets, with popular histories filling the gaps on butter and olive oil.
main: Zohary, Hopf & Weiss, *Domestication of Plants in the Old World*, for the olive and flax ([[ec2]], [[ec3]]).
Bedigian (ed.), *Sesame: The Genus Sesamum*, with Kiple's chapter and Achaya, for sesame ([[ec4]], [[x1]], [[x2]], [[th1]]).
Bottéro, *The Oldest Cuisine in the World*, for the Babylonian recipes and butter ([[e1]], [[ec6]]).
Foxhall, Kiple, Mueller and Khosrova for the olive's Bronze Age and for butter ([[te2]], [[ec8]], [[ec1]]).
Dunne et al. (through a search abstract) and Kiple for Saharan dairying and the peanut ([[ec10]], [[ec12]]); Lynn and one unverified abstract for the African oil palm ([[ec11]]).
Roffet-Salque et al., as abstracted, for Neolithic beeswax ([[ec16]]).

Lucas for Egypt’s fats and oils, read from a scanned copy by OCR ([[ec19]], [[ec20]], [[ec21]], [[ec7]]); Chang and Anderson for China ([[ec22]], [[th5]]); Suryanarayan 2021 and Fuller 2006 for the Indus ([[ec17]], [[th3]]); Sherratt 1983 for milking ([[th4]]); Kirch for Near Oceania ([[ec18]]); VanDerwarker 2025 for the avocado ([[ec23]]).
Bray (SCC 6.2) and Chang for the Banpo brassica seeds and the doubted early peanut ([[ec24]], [[th5]]).
Kiple’s editors for the missing herds of the tsetse belt and the Americas ([[th6]]).
Zohary, Hopf & Weiss for poppy, Camelina and the cruciferous oil seeds ([[ec26]], [[ec25]], [[ec27]]).
contested: The Akkadian 'oil-plant' as sesame rather than flax ([[th1]]); older statements that no sesame came from Mesopotamia are corrected by later finds ([[x1]]).
Palm fat at Abydos rests on one analysis of 1897 ([[ec7]]).
Palace oil stores at Ebla, Mari and Ugarit come from a journalist's summary ([[ec9]]).
The soybean's Chinese dating ([[ec14]]) and the Babylonian soap claim ([[te3]]) are unsettled.
Saharan dairy fat rests on an abstract and press coverage, not the paper ([[ec10]]); the oil-palm shells on one abstract ([[ec11]]); the identity of nhh is argued ([[th2]]).
The blubber lamps are known here only by an article title and context ([[te4]]); the Baltic lipid study only by its abstract ([[ec15]]).
Beeswax shows use of the honeybee, not beekeeping, and is a wax rather than a fat ([[ec16]]).

The Abydos palm fat is rejected by Lucas ([[ec7]]); the Chekiang sesame and peanuts are doubted by Chang and Anderson ([[th5]]); the Indus lipid result is hard to read without local reference fats ([[ec17]]).
‘An absence of animal fats’ is the editors’ general phrase and the folio’s own Saharan and hunter entries are exceptions ([[th6]]).

The Camelina dating in Zohary is internally inconsistent, ‘ca. 4,000 BC’ against the fifth and fourth millennia BP ([[ec25]]); the poppy, Camelina and brassica entries show seeds, not pressed oil ([[ec26]], [[ec25]], [[ec27]]).
gaps: Chinese oils before 1200 BC appear only as pig fat, a doubted find and a conjecture about brassica seeds ([[ec22]], [[th5]], [[ec24]]); Bray’s account of the oil crops is read for this, but not Wagner or the Chinese archaeological reports. Bray notes that the Chinese oil press is not described before the Sung.

Marine fats beyond the Baltic and Japan — the Arctic, the Pacific coasts, the Indian Ocean fish-eaters, Moseley’s Andean coast — are not covered; African fats other than the palm and Saharan milk (shea, Ethiopian oilseeds) are missing.
The Egyptian entries rest on Lucas, who wrote in the 1920s–60s; later work on Egyptian oils (Serpico & White) is not held.

how_to_read: Read the thesis and the big ideas first, then the threads: each runs in date order and points to the entries that carry it. Entries that no thread needs are still reached through the regional picture and the lists.

Start with *Economy* and *Exchange*, where the crops are, then *Technology* for the presses and for rendering. The fat groups run through the folio (Olive Oil, Oilseeds, Butter & Ghee, Palm & Coconut), so a reader can follow one substance across periods.
Most lanes are empty by design: there is almost no evidence for law, belief or conflict about fats before 1200 BC. The next folio is where the olive and sesame get states, gods and laws.

The *picture by region* counts the 44 entries: Europe 6, Near East 19, Far East 9, Africa 2, Americas 4, Oceania 1, Worldwide 3. Egypt, China, India, the Americas and Oceania each now have entries drawn from books or papers read, though the Near East still carries most and Africa has only two.
